actions.justification: Mandatory action: Hydration status assessment is critical prior to contrast administration in a CKD stage 4 patient. Adequate pre-hydration is a cornerstone of CIN prevention.

Mandatory action: Baseline eGFR must be established before contrast exposure to quantify renal risk, guide contrast volume limits, and establish reference for post-procedure monitoring in this CKD stage 4 patient.

Mandatory action: Review of risk factors (CKD stage 4, diabetes, potential nephrotoxin use, hemodynamic status) is required to stratify CIN risk and plan preventive measures before cardiac catheterization.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned cardiac catheterization — reassess current hemodynamic status to guide pre-procedural optimization and contrast risk stratification.
Review current medications (especially nephrotoxins like NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) that may need to be held before contrast administration in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume limit based on eGFR (CKD stage 4) to minimize contrast-induced nephropathy risk during cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both high-risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy prior to cardiac catheterization. Nephrology consultation is indicated for guidance on contrast use, pre-procedure optimization, and renal protection strategies.

Given CKD stage 4 (significantly reduced GFR) and diabetes, evaluating whether alternative imaging modalities (e.g., CT without contrast, MRI) can achieve diagnostic goals while minimizing nephrotoxic contrast exposure is a key safety step.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for acute kidney injury. Identifying and discontinuing nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors if appropriate) before contrast administration is a critical preventive measure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin) prior to cardiac catheterization is a guideline-recommended step to reduce AKI risk.
Baseline eGFR has been assessed; formally documenting the eGFR check is required for procedural clearance and risk stratification before contrast administration in a patient with CKD stage 4.

Monitoring urine output in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4 + diabetes) prior to catheterization helps assess volume status and baseline renal perfusion, guiding pre-procedural hydration decisions.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization requires IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (e.g., normal saline or sodium bicarbonate) pre-procedure to reduce contrast-induced nephropathy risk, per nephroprotective guidelines.

Metformin should be held prior to contrast administration in patients with CKD stage 4 due to risk of lactic acidosis if contrast-induced AKI occurs, per standard contrast nephropathy prevention guidelines.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes; review and adjust all renally-dosed medications appropriately before procedure to minimize additional nephrotoxic burden.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is undergoing contrast exposure. Holding nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) perioperatively reduces additive renal injury risk per CIN prevention guidelines.

Post-contrast IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CIN prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes). Should be initiated/planned immediately after contrast administration.
CIN is defined as a rise in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥25% from baseline at 48 hours post-contrast. Scheduling this check is mandatory for monitoring in this high-risk patient.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. IV hydration before contrast administration is a key preventive measure per CI-AKI guidelines.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of contrast-induced AKI.
Patient has CKD stage 4 (G3b or worse), and metformin should be held around the time of contrast administration to prevent lactic acidosis risk.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Monitoring serum creatinine at 48-72 hours post-contrast is essential to detect CI-AKI per standard guidelines. The 48h check has been done; continued serial monitoring through 72h is warranted.
Per CI-AKI guidelines, serum creatinine should be rechecked at 72 hours post-contrast in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes) to confirm whether AKI has developed or is resolving.

Optimizing fluid status is a key ongoing intervention in CIN prevention and management for high-risk CKD patients post-contrast exposure. Ensuring adequate hydration supports renal perfusion and reduces AKI risk.
